title: Celebrity and humanitarian advocates of persecuted Nigerian Christians hope for continued attention to crisis
excerpt:
Celebrities such as Nicki Minaj have spoken out about the persecution of Nigerian Christians as advocates worry about renewed violence.  (Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images)

While humanitarian groups ...
body_text:
Celebrities such as Nicki Minaj have spoken out about the persecution of Nigerian Christians as advocates worry about renewed violence.  (Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images)

While humanitarian groups and celebrities have condemned attacks on Nigerian Christians, reports of renewed violence in the country's Middle Belt and concerns about the political fallout from the U.S. midterm elections have raised concerns about the future of religious-freedom efforts.

Advocates question whether the violence will subside and hope for more attention to the crisis.

"Things have gotten worse," Stephen Osemwegie, president and founder of Save Nigeria Group USA, a nonprofit focused on the welfare of Nigerians in America and around the world, told Fox News Digital. "So as far as the scale, yes, people are still getting killed, but it's not making the news because the U.S. is a bit distracted."

He said millions of people remain displaced, churches continue to be vandalized and destroyed, and parishioners are being killed while the war in Iran and the recent midterm elections have dominated U.S. headlines.

BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: THE WAR ON CHRISTIANS IS REAL AND THE WORLD CAN NO LONGER STAY SILENT

While religious and communal strife has existed for decades, the violent conflict involving Islamist insurgencies began around 2009. Since then, the United Nations and Armed Conflict & Location Data Project (ACLED), which monitors conflict and protest, reports that violence across Nigeria has claimed upwards of 53,000+ lives across communities. Advocacy and human rights groups like Intersociety and Open Doors report that over 50,000 to 62,000 Christians have been killed since 2009.

Beyond humanitarian organizations, Christian leaders and church groups, celebrities such as rapper Nicki Minaj and actress Patricia Heaton have repeatedly addressed the crisis publicly.

Rev. Ezekiel Dachomo, regional leader of the Church of Christ in Nations, in Nigeria’s Middle Belt, preaching at a funeral of murdered Christians. (Truth Nigeria/ Masara Kim)

In October, during an X Takeover event at Tesla's Giga Texas facility, Minaj spoke about her personal connection to Nigeria and urged fellow celebrities, influencers and Christians to raise awareness of the crisis.

In November 2025, she joined U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz at an event titled "Combatting Religious Violence and the Killing of Christians in Nigeria," where she delivered remarks and thanked President Donald Trump for his efforts prioritizing the issue, combatting extremism and trying to put a stop to violence to those who want to exercise their natural right to freedom of religion or belief.

"I stand here as a proud New Yorker with a deep sense of gratitude that we live in a country where we can freely and safely worship God regardless of one's creed, background or politics. No group should ever be persecuted for practicing their religion…," Minaj said. "In Nigeria, Christians are being targeted, driven from their homes and killed. Churches have been burned, families have been torn apart, and entire communities live in fear constantly simply because of how they pray."

NIGERIAN PASTOR HIGHLIGHTED BY TRUMP SAYS HE’S NEXT AFTER MILITIA KILLS HIS RELATIVES

Likewise, Heaton has shared social media posts and news commentary about reported massacres, beheadings and mass burials. She has also criticized what she sees as insufficient media coverage and international attention.

In May, she wrote "Pray for our brothers and sisters" while re-posting a video by Jeremy Wayne Tate noting that more than 70% of all Christians killed for their faith last year were Nigerian.

US, NIGERIA STRIKE ISIS FIGHTERS AGAIN FROM THE AIR AFTER KILLING SENIOR LEADER

Young Nigerians protest killings following attacks on Christian-majority villages in Benue state in June 2025. (Open Doors UK)

Fox News Digital reached out to both Minaj and Heaton for additional comment.

Violence stemming from clashes and attacks by radical Islamist groups, including Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), as well as Fulani ethnic militias, has intensified since the 2010s. Attacks have increasingly extended into Nigeria's Middle Belt, targeting farming and Christian communities, while the crisis exists within a broader national conflict that has affected communities across religious lines, including Muslims and others.

Organizations such as Open Doors International that monitor the crisis report that thousands of Christians have been displaced and forced into camps within the country. Meanwhile, Sahara Reporters cited an October report by Aid to the Church in Need that said more than 3.5 million people had been displaced in Nigeria.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

A recent report by the news and investigative media project Truth Nigeria questioned whether Nigerian Christian leaders are reconsidering their Washington strategy following the midterm elections. It examined concerns that Republican lawmakers who supported Nigeria's Country of Particular Concern (CPC) redesignation and stricter accountability measures have now lost political influence, leaving local leaders to navigate the crisis.

While Osemwegie credited the Trump administration for highlighting the situation and designating Nigeria as a Country of Particular Concern (CPC) — particularly through cooperation between the two countries on drone surveillance and intelligence sharing — he remains concerned about potential changes in congressional pressure, religious-freedom advocacy and calls for accountability.

Osemwegie hopes that American assistance remains because of the country's "vast experience dealing with global terror."

"We're hoping we can get attention to sustain some of the gains that have been recently made," he said.

ISIS TERROR LEADER AT LARGE AFTER US STRIKE KILLS TOP COMMANDER AMID RISING AFRICA THREAT: ANALYST

Catholics gather for Mass at the Church of the Assumption in Lagos, Nigeria, on April 21, 2025. (Olympia De Maismont/AFP)

"We want that to continue. We don't want a relapse. So those are some of the things we're advocating for," he said.

The House Foreign Affairs Committee's Africa Subcommittee held a hearing Thursday titled "One Year Later: Assessing Nigeria's Efforts to Protect Christians and Secure the Middle Belt" chaired by Rep. Chris Smith, R-N.J. The hearing's title references the Nov. 20, 2025, Africa Subcommittee hearing on religious persecution in Nigeria.

The Center for Strategic and International Studies covered the hearing and said that the focus on Christian persecution was important, but also noted the large loss of Muslim life in the country; the United Nations has reported more Muslims have been killed overall in the country.

"The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom’s 2026 Annual Report described religious freedom conditions during 2025 as 'abysmal,' documenting attacks on Christians and authorities’ failures to respond, investigate, or pursue justice. It also reports attacks on Muslims and practitioners of traditional religions, including Muslims killed by insurgents in Sokoto and Borno state," the CSIS wrote.

title: How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
excerpt:
Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy

A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast...
body_text:
Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy

A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.

On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.

For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.

With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.

Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.

But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.

It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

The city-state has had some success in policing this.

It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.

They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.

In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.

The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.

Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.

But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.

Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.

In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.

Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.

Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.

In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.

Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.

Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.

On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".

China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.

Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following a board meeting

How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.

In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.

For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.

But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.

Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.

BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.

In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.

Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.

During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.

Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.

Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.

Alice Huang, seen here in Taipei with Jensen Huang last year, ran Megaspeed for several months in 2023

All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore.

"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.

Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".

But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.

With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.

Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.

Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said.

"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.

But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China".

"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."

Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.

How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?

How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions

title: FAA ground stop leaves College Football teams stranded on eve of crucial Saturday showdowns
excerpt: FOX Business correspondent Grady Trimble provides a firsthand account of the nationwide FAA ground stop while stranded aboard a plane at Chicago O'hare International Airport. Trimble describes the sit...
body_text:
FOX Business correspondent Grady Trimble provides a firsthand account of the nationwide FAA ground stop while stranded aboard a plane at Chicago O'hare International Airport. Trimble describes the situation on the tarmac as flights are halted across the country, raising concerns about widespread travel disruptions and delays.

The FAA ground stop that was issued on Friday afternoon is obviously having an effect on travel across the country, but it's also having a major impact on college football teams scheduled to play on Saturday.

The second nationwide ground stop since 9/11 could disrupt travel over the next few days as passengers wait for the FAA to allow flights to resume ahead of a busy travel weekend.

But concern is growing across college athletics for teams that have yet to depart for Saturday’s games.

MISSISSIPPI STATE’S KAMARIO TAYLOR FINALIZING A REPORTED $7.5 MILLION DEAL, IN WILD COLLEGE FOOTBALL MOVE

According to multiple sources, some of those schools who are currently looking for alternative travel include Texas, Tennessee, Ole Miss, Washington, Minnesota, Baylor, Tulane, Auburn, Arizona State, Oregon State and others.

USC has already taken off for their trip to Bloomington for a showdown with Indiana, and are currently in the air.

Head coach Steve Sarkisian of the Texas Longhorns watches action during a game against the Oklahoma Sooners at Cotton Bowl on October 10, 2026, in Dallas, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) (Stacy Revere/Getty Images)

For instance, Texas was scheduled to depart Austin and had already boarded its plane for Baton Rouge ahead of Saturday's showdown against LSU, but the FAA had issued the ground stop before they had taken off for Louisiana.

In the case of a school like Tennessee, the Vols were scheduled to depart McGee Tyson Airport in Knoxville at 4 p.m. ET, but the FAA notice was issued, and the team was not able to get into the air. How they end up getting to College Station is still to be determined at this moment, though the situation remains fluid.

Other schools across the country were lucky under the circumstances, and had already departed for their road game destination.

WEEK 8 AP TOP 25 POLL SEES BIG TEN GAIN EQUAL FOOTING ON SEC AND UNBEATEN UTAH EARN MAJOR RESPECT

Some schools also had the luxury to take buses to their game, like Alabama traveling to Nashville for its game against Vanderbilt.

This could turn out to be the case for a team like Auburn, who is scheduled to play Mississippi State on Saturday in Starkville.

But, for No. 2 Utah, the Utes were grounded in Salt Lake City before they were scheduled to take off for their matchup with Arizona on Saturday night.

Schools typically travel on Friday afternoons for Saturday games, usually holding a walkthrough at their facility before heading straight to the airport for departure.

Tennessee Volunteers running back Daune Morris (17) runs against the Alabama Crimson Tide during the second half at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville, Tenn., on Oct. 17, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Also, most schools will have security checkpoints actually set up at their facilities, so they can just get off the bus and board the airplane that is taking them to their destination.

This is a developing story, and we will continue to provide updates here at OutKick and Fox News.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

title: 32 passengers taken to hospital after tanker hits river cruise boat in US
excerpt:
Dozens of passengers have been taken to hospital after a tanker struck a river cruise boat carrying 129 passengers in New Orleans, partially submerging the vessel, according to authorities.

The Atlan...
body_text:
Dozens of passengers have been taken to hospital after a tanker struck a river cruise boat carrying 129 passengers in New Orleans, partially submerging the vessel, according to authorities.

The Atlantic Asphalt tanker hit the American Heritage paddleboat on the Mississippi River on Friday at about 12:30pm local time (18:30 GMT), the Port of New Orleans said.

The cruise boat had docked about two hours earlier to begin letting passengers off.

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference on Friday evening that all passengers on board the American Heritage were accounted for and that 32 were in local hospitals, none with critical injuries.

The Atlantic Asphalt tanker “lost control and collided into the cruise ship”, she said.

Passengers were disembarking when the boat “began to sink, and then eventually toppled over and flipped”, sending people into the water, she said.

Video from the scene showed the much larger tanker hitting the paddlewheel cruise boat as metal and glass crashed and crunched, according to The Associated Press news agency.

More than a dozen people in life jackets were dragged from the river, where the water temperature was 19 degrees Celsius (66 degrees Fahrenheit), onto nearby ships, while others stood near the railing as the boat listed further into the water.

“Surreal, that’s what that was,” one witness, Jamie Holford, told local television. “Fifteen minutes from impact to where it rolled over.”

Port police, the fire department, the coastguard and emergency medical staff are on the scene, and a triage area was set up inside the port’s administration building. The river was closed to vessel traffic.

American Cruise Lines, which operates the boat, said guests and crew had been evacuated and that it was “deeply concerned for everyone involved”.

The five-deck American Heritage, built in 2015, holds up to 150 passengers and was finishing an eight-day cruise to destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.

The 160-metre (520-foot) tanker was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands and was bound for New Orleans, according to the MarineTraffic tracker. It specialises in carrying asphalt and bitumen, according to the maritime periodical Marine Insights.

The cause of the collision, as well as whether the ship was carrying cargo, remains unknown.

title: UFC boss Dana White brushes off Democratic probe threats, recalls 'crazy 48 hours' around Trump job offer
excerpt: Dana White speaks out on 'My View with Lara Trump' on the Democrats potentially targeting allies of President Trump after their midterm wins. The full interview airs Saturday at 9 p.m. ET on Fox News....
body_text:
Dana White speaks out on 'My View with Lara Trump' on the Democrats potentially targeting allies of President Trump after their midterm wins. The full interview airs Saturday at 9 p.m. ET on Fox News.

UFC CEO Dana White dismissed concerns about a potential congressional investigation by Democrats, saying he is not worried about being targeted over his close ties to President Donald Trump.

In a preview of "My View with Lara Trump," set to air in full on Saturday at 9 p.m. ET, White said he expects Democrats to go after him.

"Well, I mean, we kind of expected that," White said when asked by Fox News host Lara Trump if he was worried about being targeted by Democrats.

BERNIE SANDERS WARNS DEMOCRATS NOT TO SPEND ALL THEIR TIME INVESTIGATING TRUMP

UFC CEO Dana White takes questions from reporters during a press briefing with President Donald Trump in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)

"If you didn't do anything illegal or anything wrong, I don't know why you'd have to be worried. I've never done anything in the political world that would be illegal, where anybody should come after me or anything that we have to hide. I expect it, but no, I'm not worried about it."

The exchange comes as Democrats prepare their oversight agenda following the Nov. 3 midterms. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, recently warned Trump administration officials and allies to "lawyer up" ahead of potential investigations.

White has been an outspoken supporter of President Trump and joined him in the White House briefing room Monday, where he addressed reporters. During the interview, White described the experience as "incredible."

JACKSON THOMPSON: DANA WHITE SAYS HE'LL MEET WITH TRUMP AMID CLAIM OF WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY JOB OFFER

"No, it was incredible. What an amazing experience. Literally, when I was pulling in the gates of the White House, his assistant called and said, ‘Hey, we're going to take you right down to the press room. He wants you in the house,’" White said.

"This is crazy. It was a very unique and crazy 48 hours for me."

President Trump posted Nov. 7 on Truth Social that he had offered White the White House press secretary position following Katie Zacharia's departure, prompting some questions.

"I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States," the commander in chief wrote in the post. "Dana, please take the job!"

TRUMP'S NEW PRESS SECRETARY OUT OF THE JOB JUST DAYS AFTER ROCKY DEBUT

UFC CEO Dana White and President Donald Trump appear during a news conference in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Tierney L. Cross/The Washington Post/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

TRUMP CLOSING IN ON NEW PRESS SECRETARY AS ADMINISTRATION OFFICIALS PUSH FOR PICK WHO COULD BREAK THE MOLD

Both President Trump and White addressed the post during Monday's briefing, and the president explained he was only joking.

"We were having a very bad press day, and I said, 'I don't know why I thought of his name.' He's been my friend for a long time. I said, 'You know, I think I'm going to get Dana White to be my new press secretary,'" President Trump told reporters.

"I said it to a group of the press, and that was it. I was sort of kidding, and then they wrote the story as though I wasn't kidding."

"I have zero political aspirations," White said. "I was at a fight for Zuffa Boxing in London when he called me and told me that he had done this, and the last 24 hours of my life have been insane."

President Donald Trump and UFC president and CEO Dana White enter the octagon after a lightweight championship fight during UFC Freedom 250 on the South Lawn of the White House June 14, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Jeff Bottari/Zuffa LLC via Getty Images)

White’s ties to President Trump have drawn attention in recent years, with White speaking at the past three Republican National Conventions. He also partnered with the White House to stage UFC Freedom 250 on the South Lawn, described as the first professional sporting event ever held at the presidential residence.

DANA WHITE SAYS 'I DON'T GIVE A S---' IF TRUMP FRIENDSHIP COSTS HIM BUSINESS, 250TH EVENT WAS TRUMP'S IDEA

Fox News Digital’s Louis Casiano contributed to this report.

To watch Fox News host Lara Trump's full interview with UFC CEO Dana White, tune in Saturday at 9 p.m. ET to 'My View with Lara Trump.'

Madison Colombo is a writer for Fox News Digital’s Flash, Media, and Culture team, covering daily breaking news and trending topics with an award-winning background in broadcast and digital journalism.

title: Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of ‘racist’ campaign against Israel’s Arab minority
excerpt:
Statement is rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis

Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot accused caretaker premier Benjamin ...
body_text:
Statement is rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis

Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot accused caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fuelling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab minority, after he sought to delegitimise the community’s lawmakers by linking them to Hamas.

Eisenkot’s statement was a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis, who make up more than 20% of the population.

Two Arab-majority parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, secured a combined 19 seats in last month’s election, winning nearly a sixth of the 120-seat parliament and potentially emerging as kingmakers in efforts by Eisenkot to form a government.

“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” Eisenkot wrote on X on Friday.

“They have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation, fuelled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” he added.

“The attempt to marginalise them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of civic responsibility.”

Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly criticised leaders of Arab parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a “terror group” after its unprecedented 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.

All leaders of Arab parties have condemned the attack, in which Arab Israelis – descendants of Palestinians who remained in what became Israel in 1948 – were also among those killed.

Netanyahu has also repeatedly alleged electoral fraud by Arab-majority parties, but electoral authorities have rejected the claims.

In a speech, Netanyahu lamented that the two Arab lists refused to recognise Israel as a Jewish state, although Ra’am’s leader, Mansour Abbas, has done so in the past.

He further claimed that they sought to establish either an “Islamic state” or a “nationalist Palestinian state”.

During the same ceremony, the national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, heckled Joint List’s leader, Yousef Jabareen, during his oath of allegiance, accusing him of having “pledged allegiance to Hamas”.

“It is entirely legitimate to disagree with representatives of the Arab parties, even to strongly disapprove of some of them. But it is neither legitimate nor acceptable to malign an entire community, and I will not allow it,” Eisenkot said.

President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a new government on Sunday after consultations in which a majority of political parties, including the two Arab lists, recommended him for the role.

But one of Eisenkot’s rightwing allies, Avigdor Lieberman, has said he will back out of the coalition if Arab Israelis are part of it.

If Eisenkot fails to form a government within 28 days, he may request a 14-day extension. Should he still fall short, the mandate would pass to another lawmaker, most likely Netanyahu.

title: Hungary seizes $19.5m in cash found buried in forests amid graft inquiry
excerpt:
Anti-corruption agency carried out searches as part of investigation into Orbán-era minister accused of taking bribes

Hungary’s anti-corruption agency said on Friday it had seized cash worth $19.5m (...
body_text:
Anti-corruption agency carried out searches as part of investigation into Orbán-era minister accused of taking bribes

Hungary’s anti-corruption agency said on Friday it had seized cash worth $19.5m (£14.8m) buried in forests and hidden elsewhere while investigating an ex-minister of nationalist former leader Viktor Orbán’s cabinet.

Miklós Seszták, Hungary’s minister of national development between 2014 and 2018, is accused of taking bribes in a scheme involving the state transport company, purchasing secondhand buses at inflated prices.

The prime minister, Péter Magyar, won a landslide election victory in April, ending Orbán’s 16 years in power after promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of office during his rival’s rule.

Seszták, two other Orbán-era ministers and the former premier’s brother have been taken into custody in different cases as graft inquiries have gathered pace in recent weeks.

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH), an anti-graft body with sweeping powers established as part of Magyar’s accountability drive, said it searched several locations on Thursday and Friday as part of the criminal proceedings against Seszták.

“During the search, investigators found large amounts of cash: buried in forests, hidden in agricultural and warehouse buildings as well as residential properties, and stored in high-value safes in secluded locations,” the statement said.

“The total amount of cash found during the two-day search was 5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and US $1,257,100,” it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m.

NVVH said its staff deposited the cash into the Hungarian State Treasury’s account.

“Upon receipt, 12 Treasury employees spent 8 hours counting the money using 5 counting machines,” the finance minister, András Kármán, said on Facebook.

Magyar hailed the seizure as a potential turning point.

“This officially marks the end of the Fidesz-KDNP mafia!” he said in reference to Orbán’s former governing coalition.

The former leader did not react to the latest development. Orbán had previously denounced the probes targeting his inner circle as “political persecution” aimed at imprisoning him.

title: Sophie Cunningham laughs at Stephen A Smith's belittling claim about White NBA players
excerpt: On this episode of Don't @ Me with Dan Dakich, we dive into the MASSIVE media feud over the Los Angeles Lakers' newly formed trio. Skip Bayless completely shut down Stephen A. Smith's viral and racial...
body_text:
On this episode of Don't @ Me with Dan Dakich, we dive into the MASSIVE media feud over the Los Angeles Lakers' newly formed trio. Skip Bayless completely shut down Stephen A. Smith's viral and racially motivated criticism of the new trio

Luka Doncic is on pace for one of the greatest seasons in NBA history, averaging just under 40 points per game. WNBA star Sophie Cunningham loves watching him set these records, especially when he makes Stephen A. Smith look like a clown in the process.

This week, Smith again said the Los Angeles Lakers cannot win an NBA championship led by "three White dudes": Doncic, Austin Reaves and Walker Kessler. He said they need more "brothers" to help them.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"He’s killing it," she said on her "No Hesitation" podcast about Doncic’s historic start to the season. "He has been so much fun to watch."

"Stephen A. was, like, ‘Why would the Lakers ever build a team around three White boys? Like, look at the NBA history. That’s never going to happen. That’s never going to be successful.’ And he (Doncic) is out there freaking killing it. I think it’s so funny."

Also funny: In the very season Smith is belittling the idea of building around three White players, the Lakers’ trio ranks as the NBA’s best, according to ESPN’s own advanced analytics.

WILL CAIN CHALLENGES STEPHEN A SMITH ON 'RACIST' CLAIM ABOUT 'WHITE DUDES' IN THE NBA

Stephen A. Smith attends a basketball game between the Los Angeles Lakers and the New York Knicks at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, Calif., on March 6, 2025. (Allen Berezovsky/Getty Images)

As OutKick explained this week, Doncic, Reaves and Kessler are not the reason the Lakers have only the 10th-best championship odds. Based on their play alone, Los Angeles would be near the top. The concern is the weak supporting cast around them.

Here’s the catch: Those role players are almost entirely Black.

If Stephen A. insists on blaming the Lakers’ championship limitations on a particular race, he’s blaming the wrong one.

The truth can be uncomfortable, can’t it?

Cunningham should laugh at Smith’s statement. It’s laughable. It’s wrong. And it sounds like he’s trying far too hard to appease the people who criticize his coverage of Black athletes.

title: Tennessee running back breaks leg in single-vehicle crash, school says, putting season in doubt
excerpt: The Buffalo Bills beat the Baltimore Ravens 36-10, and Lamar Jackson suffered a thumb injury that put him in Injured Reserve. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask if the Ravens’ season i...
body_text:
The Buffalo Bills beat the Baltimore Ravens 36-10, and Lamar Jackson suffered a thumb injury that put him in Injured Reserve. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask if the Ravens’ season is over, if Jackson has played his final snap with the Ravens, and they discuss the Denver Broncos beating the Kansas City Chiefs 28-24.

A Tennessee football player's season in jeopardy after he lost control of his car and broke his leg in a single-vehicle crash.

Running back Daune Morris, fresh off a big game against then-No. 6 Kentucky that saved the Volunteers' season, now faces doubt on whether or not he will be able to play the rest of the year over something that may have been avoidable.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

According to reports, citing records from the Knoxville Police Department, Morris' car hit a fire hydrant and rolled onto its side, while also hitting four other cars.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Daune Morris #17 of the Tennessee Volunteers runs the ball for a touchdown during the NCAA football game between the University of Tennessee Volunteers and the University of Kentucky Wildcats at Neyland Stadium, Knoxville, TN Tim Gangloff/CSM/Sipa USA (Credit Image: Tim Gangloff/Cal Sport Media/Sipa USA) (Tim Gangloff/Cal Sport Media/Sipa USA)

Morris apparently told police he lost control of his car while making a right turn trying to accelerate early Friday morning. The car, a 2021 Dodge Charger, eventually came to rest on its roof.

He was taken to the UT Medical Center with minor injuries.

The school said Morris suffered a broken leg.

"Tennessee running back Daune Morris was involved in a one-vehicle accident off campus early Friday morning," the school said in a statement. "He sustained non-life-threatening injuries, including a broken leg, and is resting comfortably. We wish Daune the best in his recovery."

Tennessee Volunteers running back Daune Morris (17) runs against the Alabama Crimson Tide during the second half at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville, Tenn., on Oct. 17, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

The Knoxville News said Morris was also cited last month for speeding and failure to exercise due care as a driver.

Police did not immediately respond to an email from OutKick.

Morris has rushed for 434 yards and three touchdowns this season, including a 66-yard score in the first quarter of last week's 34-6 win over the Wildcats. Tennessee entered the game No. 13 in the College Football Playoff rankings.

Tennessee Volunteers running back Daune Morris (17) carries the ball for a touchdown against the Kentucky Wildcats during the first quarter at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville, Tenn., on Nov. 7, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

The win put the Volunteers at the No. 8 seed in the bracket, and they now undoubtedly control their own destiny to play in the postseason. However, they may have to do it without Morris.

title: Washington Democrat AG hands girls’ sports law defense to outside firm amid conflict of interest concerns
excerpt:
Seattle’s school board unanimously authorized potential legal action Monday against a voter-approved measure barring biological males from girls’ school sports. (Credit: Seattle Public Schools)

Washi...
body_text:
Seattle’s school board unanimously authorized potential legal action Monday against a voter-approved measure barring biological males from girls’ school sports. (Credit: Seattle Public Schools)

Washington Attorney General Nick Brown has appointed an outside law firm to defend a voter-approved measure barring biological males from girls’ school sports, while his office continues its work defending transgender rights.

Brown announced Thursday that Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner will represent Washington in defending Initiative 638, which voters approved in the Nov. 3 election.

WASHINGTON AG'S OFFICE INDICATES IT WILL DEFEND GIRLS' SPORTS BALLOT MEASURE AFTER ACLU SUES TO BLOCK IT

Washington state Attorney General Nick Brown speaks to the media outside the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington in Seattle on Feb. 28, 2025, following a hearing on the state's request for a preliminary injunction against President Donald Trump's executive order attacking gender-affirming care for youth. (AFP via Getty Images)

"My personal views do not dictate what laws get defended or the strength of that defense," Brown said.

Brown described defending voter-enacted laws as a core responsibility. He also pointed to his office’s litigation protecting transgender residents’ health care and equal treatment, saying that work would continue.

He said appointing outside attorneys as special assistant attorneys general is a common practice when conflicts, expertise needs or workload prevent the office from handling a case itself. Brown described BCLP as an experienced firm with a substantial Washington presence that has previously represented the state.

The announcement follows questions from Fox News Digital about how Brown’s office would handle the defense, including connections between his office and organizations challenging the initiative.

"When a new law is passed by the people or the Legislature, our role is to ensure it is defended regardless of our personal views about the policy. We will review court filings as they come and discuss next steps," the office previously told Fox News Digital.

When asked follow-up questions, the office said it was discussing its next steps and reiterated its obligation to ensure the law is defended.

Brown’s former law firm, Pacifica Law Group, is among the organizations representing the challengers, alongside the ACLU of Washington and Legal Voice.

The groups filed a lawsuit in King County Superior Court on Monday seeking to block the initiative before its scheduled Dec. 3 effective date. Plaintiffs include families with children participating in school sports, the Washington Education Association and TransFamilies.

JACKSON THOMPSON: COLORADO GOV-ELECT PHIL WEISER SIGNALS POSSIBLE CHANGES TO GIRLS' SPORTS BALLOT MEASURE

Opponents argue the restrictions and sex-verification requirements violate state constitutional protections, including privacy and equal rights. They contend the requirements could expose girls to intrusive examinations and exclude transgender students from opportunities available to their classmates.

The initiative requires school districts and covered athletic associations to prohibit biological males from competing with or against female students in competitions designated for girls.

Students seeking to participate in those competitions must provide a form or statement signed by their personal health care provider verifying biological sex as part of their routine sports physical. The verification must rely on reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup or naturally produced testosterone levels.

The text does not require every student to undergo a genital examination. Its findings describe using the existing sports-physical process to protect fairness, safety and competitive balance in female athletics.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The measure had approximately 56% support in returns displayed by Fox News’ election results page Friday.

The court fight also comes as Seattle education officials pursue their own response. The Seattle School Board voted 7-0 Monday to authorize potential legal action concerning the measure.

Board members argued the district needed courts to clarify its obligations under the initiative and existing protections involving privacy and discrimination.

"We can’t say we’re respecting democracy if we treat the most recent vote as a reason to ignore all the other laws that are on the books," board member Joe Mizrahi said during the meeting.

That authorization was separate from the lawsuit brought by the civil rights groups and did not itself block the initiative.

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

title: Randy Travis’ wife says doctors gave country legend 1% chance of survival before miraculous comeback
excerpt:
Randy Travis' wife Mary reveals the emotional journey from a 1% survival chance to releasing "Same Old Way" more than a decade after his stroke.

Randy Travis' life was turned upside down by a devasta...
body_text:
Randy Travis' wife Mary reveals the emotional journey from a 1% survival chance to releasing "Same Old Way" more than a decade after his stroke.

Randy Travis' life was turned upside down by a devastating health crisis that doctors gave him just a 1% chance of surviving, according to his wife, Mary.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, the country legend — whose new 12-track album, "Same Old Way," is out now — and his wife, Mary, reflected on that life-changing ordeal more than a decade ago, explained how hope and faith played a pivotal role in his recovery, and shared how his determination helped him rebuild his life and reconnect with music.

"They had already told us he had 1% chance of survival. And that was the first couple of days in the hospital," Mary said. "So here we are, five and a half months later, he's still here. He's still improving. We went through the second brain surgery. He came through that with flying colors. The first one is when they said he's not, you know, he doesn't have any chance. But, you know, once you get over those and you start seeing the glimmers of hope and the hand of God on the whole thing."

RANDY TRAVIS' HEALTH CRISIS BEGAN WITH 'CONGESTION' AND ENDED IN A FIVE-MONTH HOSPITAL STAY

Randy Travis' wife, Mary, says the country legend was given a 1% chance of survival in 2013. (Getty Images for the Grand Ole Opry)

The "Forever and Ever, Amen" singer was hospitalized in 2013 for congestive heart failure tied to viral cardiomyopathy. He subsequently suffered a massive stroke that left him with partial paralysis and affected his speech. What began as a trip to seek treatment for congestion became a five-and-a-half-month hospital stay, followed by years of rehabilitation.

"We went through three years of rehab every single day, so we were very quiet and out of the limelight, if you will," she added. "We, you know, we were at home. We went to rehab every day for about three years."

Travis won many awards throughout his 40 years in the music industry, including seven Grammy Awards. (Oscar Abolafia/TPLP/Getty Images)

Eventually, Mary said, Travis "got tired" of the constant rehabilitation and decided to "go live life." Their trips back to Nashville helped renew their hope that he could once again be involved in the music he loved.

WATCH: RANDY TRAVIS’ WIFE SAYS DOCTORS GAVE COUNTRY LEGEND 1% CHANCE OF SURVIVAL BEFORE MIRACULOUS COMEBACK

Travis has since found new ways to share his music and connect with fans. In May 2024, he released "Where That Came From," using AI technology to recreate his signature singing voice. His "More Life" tour continued through 2026, with Travis appearing alongside Mary while guest vocalist James Dupré and his longtime band perform his hits.

VINCE GILL GAVE AMY GRANT A REALITY CHECK DURING RECOVERY FROM BRAIN INJURY

Mary previously told Fox News Digital that Randy's health crisis cemented their relationship. (Amy E. Price/Getty Images)

Now, with the release of his first album of original material in more than 18 years — featuring 12 previously unreleased songs recorded between 1986 and 2013 and restored by his longtime producer, Kyle Lehning — Mary is reflecting on the determination and gratitude that carried her husband through his toughest moments.

CELINE DION BREAKS DOWN ONSTAGE DURING EMOTIONAL RETURN AFTER 6-YEAR HIATUS

"Just being with this guy has been such an inspiration to me because, going through even the tough times in the hospital, the nurses would come in and cut him or stick him or poke him or do whatever, and they'd walk out the door. And if he wasn't in his coma and he was aware, he’d say, ‘Thank you.’ That was Randy Travis," she said. "And they'd turn around and look like, you got to be kidding me, you know. But that was Randy Travis."

Randy Travis, Mary Travis and James Dupré visit the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville, Tenn., on March 5, 2025. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

That same spirit, she said, followed him into rehabilitation and remains evident today, even as aphasia continues to affect his ability to communicate.

"I have pictures of him there in the rehab center and he's smiling. He's laughing. He’s giving it all he's got. Randy Travis hasn't changed. And that's still the man that I get to sit beside right now," she said. "He still has that, that love for life, the love for people."

For Mary, the release of "Same Old Way" is especially emotional because it represents an opportunity they once weren't sure would ever come again. Before his stroke, she said, they assumed there would be many more albums and years of making music ahead.

BILLY RAY CYRUS CHEATED DEATH DURING SEPSIS, VOCAL PARALYSIS BATTLE BEFORE STAGING MUSIC COMEBACK

Travis' new album, "Same Old Way," was released Nov. 13. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"It's really an emotional thing, because 18 years ago when he put out his last one, we thought that the world was an oyster and there was gonna be so many more," she said. "But the stroke happened, it was 13 years ago, and everything changed."

"Thirteen years ago, we had no idea, based on where we were then, when we were in the hospital, that we would have this opportunity. So, in a way, it’s a miracle," she added. "I get emotional when I think about it, just because I wanted to hear his voice so bad again."

Randy Travis and James Dupre perform during the Volunteer Jam: A Musical Salute to Charlie Daniels at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, Tenn., on Aug. 18, 2021. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

Hearing those recordings, Mary explained, offers listeners a chance to experience Travis' voice at different stages of his life — and gives the couple another reason to appreciate how far he has come.

"Life is so precious and so fragile, but it’s so wonderful also. And to be able to do something like this, it’s pretty monumental," she said. "It doesn't happen often that somebody has the opportunity to do this after a life-changing moment."

Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.

NBA legend Chris Bosh has been drawn into the Palisades arson case.

The defense team for Jonathan Rinderknecht is seeking testimony about a firework that allegedly launched from Bosh's property on Jan. 1, 2025, the night the Lachman Fire ignited. Rinderknecht is being retried on charges that he sparked the devastating fires, and his defense denies the allegation, citing witness accounts of fireworks as a possible cause.

His defense team is seeking to introduce testimony from Michael T. Cole, a retired California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (Cal Fire) investigator who spent 18 years in the agency’s arson unit, according to court documents obtained by the California Post. Prosecutors are seeking to disqualify Cole as a witness in a separate filing, according to the report.

NBA Hall of Famer Chris Bosh attends a game between the San Antonio Spurs and the Denver Nuggets at Moody Center in Austin, Texas, on March 15, 2024. (USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con)

"Mr. Cole is expected to testify that during his 2025 investigation of the Palisades Fire he observed and documented a mark and an associated burn and smoke trail on the driveway and rear patio area of the residence at (redacted), and that, based on his training and experience, those marks are physical evidence of a launched firework," the filing from Rinderknecht’s attorney, Steve Haney, said, according to the California Post.

The residence mentioned in the court filings belongs to Bosh, who was renting out the property when the fire broke out, according to the report.

OutKick contacted Bosh’s representatives but did not immediately receive a response.

Rinderknecht has remained in federal custody since being arrested on charges of starting the deadly blaze on Oct. 7, 2025. Investigators allegedly found a lighter in his vehicle during a search on Jan. 24, 2025.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 29, was charged with igniting the blaze that eventually became the Palisades Fire in Los Angeles. (USAttyEssayli/X)
