title: Andy Burnham urges Labour to ‘re-arm’ for Kemi Badenoch comeback
excerpt:
No 10 sources say PM wants party to refocus on Tories as electoral threat after prioritising Reform and Greens

Andy Burnham has instructed the Labour party to “re-arm” to fight the Conservatives at t...
body_text:
No 10 sources say PM wants party to refocus on Tories as electoral threat after prioritising Reform and Greens

Andy Burnham has instructed the Labour party to “re-arm” to fight the Conservatives at the next election amid concern inside government that they must take the prospect of a Kemi Badenoch-led recovery seriously.

Downing Street sources said the prime minister wanted Labour headquarters to refocus on the Tories as an electoral threat after more than two years of prioritising Nigel Farage’s Reform and, on their left flank, the Greens.

“Andy is well aware of how volatile electoral support is. Just because the Tories are trailing in the polls now, their trajectory is upwards and they could bounce back ahead of the election. We can’t be complacent about our old foe,” one source said.

The Conservatives took 24% of the vote at the last general election, before support dipped to 18%. But last week this had risen to 25%, according to polling from More in Common, the first time in 18 months they had exceeded their vote share at the time of their record election defeat.

Many Tory MPs who had felt their party’s situation was existential, now believed they had a route back, with Badenoch finally appearing to recognise that the economy, rather than culture wars, presented her with an opportunity, especially among core supporters.

A senior Downing Street figure said Burnham did not want party officials to take their eyes off Reform – which has dipped in the polls amid ongoing scrutiny of party finances – but felt they should be planning for a potential Tory resurgence as well.

A third No 10 insider told the Guardian: “Kemi is running a party base strategy with policies aimed at higher earners, mostly in the south. It won’t be enough to win at the next election but it does put them more in contention. We need to be ready for that. We need to re-arm.”

Cabinet ministers including the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, the chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, and the Europe minister Hamish Falconer have Tory-facing seats, while Labour MPs across Hertfordshire, Kent and parts of London, including Finchley and Harrow, could also be at risk.

One tactic under discussion is talking up the prospect of a Tory-Reform pact, with MPs suggesting voters would only return in earnest to the Tories if there was a genuine chance they could win a majority, but that they could stay with Labour if they were worried about Farage getting close to power.

Another is to focus on the Tory brand – including the shadow cabinet – more generally. While Badenoch’s personal ratings are relatively strong, the Conservatives overall lag way behind. A third of people who told More in Common they believed Badenoch was doing a good job, still said they would not vote for her party.

Labour officials insisted that, as the Conservatives were the official opposition, they still had them in their sights day to day. But they acknowledged they needed to step up their wider strategy.

The party is understood to be preparing to devote more resources to taking on the Tories from January, in the run-up to the May elections. “We did really well at this set of elections last time, so it will be a real test point for whether the Tories have got their act together,” one said.

A group of London MPs has urged Burnham to refocus on Badenoch’s party, which in some polls has overtaken Reform into second place, warning him that Labour HQ was “getting caught out” by “obsessing” about Reform and the Greens.

One minister with a slim majority said they had been “banging this drum” inside government for a while. “It’s time to wake up about it, frankly. I think lots of my colleagues under threat from Reform have seen some of us in more traditional Tory seats as having it easy but by the next election it could be the other way around.”

One former Keir Starmer staffer said: “Every arm of the Labour party has been refocused to take on Reform; all the strategic decisions have been taken with that in mind. That can change if the party starts the work now but it does need to start properly.”

Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common, said Burnham was right to broaden the party’s focus. “Starmer was fighting on one front, but Labour now has two fronts on its right flank. They need to prepare for all outcomes,” he said.

“Reform has shown an ability to squeeze the Conservatives but it definitely has limits, so they’re definitely going to be on the pitch at the next election.”

Tryl suggested the biggest risk to Labour was “self-sorting” by voters, with Reform winning right-leaning votes from Labour in the “red wall”, while the Conservatives took them in affluent parts of England, including the south-east.

“Because of the shallow but broad nature of Labour’s support at the last election, there are more seats that could end up being Labour-Tory fights than you might think,” he said, adding that the Tories were also currently taking more votes from the Lib Dems than the other way around.

title: Chris Van Hollen floats using government shutdown threat to force Trump to end Iran war
excerpt:
Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen floated using a government shutdown threat to end the war in Iran during an interview on Thursday.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., floated using a government shutdown t...
body_text:
Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen floated using a government shutdown threat to end the war in Iran during an interview on Thursday.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., floated using a government shutdown to get President Donald Trump to end the war in Iran during an interview on Thursday, after announcing he would challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the incoming Majority Leader position.

Van Hollen was asked multiple times during an MS NOW interview how he would be different from Schumer as leader. The senator pointed to ending the war in Iran.

"Well, the difference is, I believe we need to be firm," he said. "I think that we heard loud and clear from the American people that they want to end the war in Iran and bring down prices. We shouldn't say we're going to wait until January when we have the power to do it on Dec. 11. And so, this should not be a finger in the wind issue. This should not be sort of frittering around. This should not be a question of timidity. We need to answer the call of the American people, end the war, bring down prices, do it now. Not a penny, not a penny to fuel this war."

Congress will need to fund the government by Dec. 11 to avoid a shutdown. MS NOW's Jen Psaki asked Van Hollen if Trump would be "forced" to end the war because Congress couldn't do it unilaterally.

FOX NEWS POLL: 71% THINK TRUMP ADMINISTRATION LACKS PLAN TO END IRAN WAR

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, is hoping to be the next Senate Majority Leader. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"The president would be given a choice, right? Does he say to the American people that 'I'm going to shut down the United States government? Am I going to shut down all the agencies of the U.S. government to keep the illegal war in Iran going and to keep prices high,' when we could do it now?" Van Hollen said.

He said Trump could choose to "completely ignore" the will of the American people and shut down the government.

Schumer's office did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment. The White House also did not return a request for comment.

SEN BERNIE SANDERS SUPPORTS CHRIS VAN HOLLEN'S BID TO CHALLENGE SCHUMER FOR SENATE DEMOCRATIC LEADER POST

Van Hollen announced Thursday he would challenge Schumer for the Majority Leader position after Democrats won back the chamber in the 2026 midterms.

"In this election, the American people called for change," Van Hollen said in a statement. "They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies — but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people."

Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen reacts while speaking to Secretary of State Marco Rubio as he testifies at a Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing on May 20, 2025. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

SCHUMER'S GRIP ON POWER SLIPS AS DEMS BEGIN TO REVOLT AGAINST HIM, EYE NEW LEADERSHIP

"It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," he continued. "This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader."

Van Hollen, 67, has served in Congress for 23 years, beginning his career in the House before moving to the Senate in 2017. Schumer, 75, has been in Congress since 1981.

Liz Mair, a Republican strategist and head of Mair Strategies, told Fox News Digital in a statement, that the shutdown position could be an "effective strategy" for the Democrats.

"If you do want to force the Pentagon's hand, this is the easiest way to do it, legislatively, right?" she said. "I think the question is how much reputational downside is there for Democrats?"

"Progressives seem to put in quite a lot of confidence in Chris Van Hollen as a prospective leader. And I just wonder whether that's wise on their part," she added, questioning if Van Hollen could execute it.

Chuck Schumer already has several incoming senators who are against him being Majority Leader in the new Congress. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

Van Hollen's decision to challenge Schumer comes as several members of the Senate have said they won't support the latter.

Longtime allies such as Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and newer members such as Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., declared this week that they would not back Schumer for leader.

CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'

Several senators-elect who rode the blue wave to Washington, D.C., have publicly said they will not support Schumer for leader. Senators-elect Adam Hamilton, Kan., Peggy Flanagan, and Abdul El-Sayed have all publicly rejected the longtime New York senator as the Democratic leader.

Van Hollen said he would prioritize restoring Medicaid funding, extending the Affordable Care Act's tax credits, and restoring food and nutrition programs when asked about what he would do in his first 100 days as leader.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Van Hollen also criticized Schumer for endorsing moderate candidates in Democratic primaries.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks during a press conference at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee headquarters on Nov. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Tom Brenner/Getty Images)

Hanna Panreck is an associate editor at Fox News.

title: Labour chief whip tells Vogue she takes tough approach to keeping MPs in line
excerpt:
Anneliese Midgley surprises colleagues after Burnham said whips’ office should not be ‘something to be feared’

If Andy Burnham has been accused of being a people pleaser by his critics, the same most...
body_text:
Anneliese Midgley surprises colleagues after Burnham said whips’ office should not be ‘something to be feared’

If Andy Burnham has been accused of being a people pleaser by his critics, the same most certainly cannot be said of his chief whip.

“I’m not going to take any shit and I don’t fuck about,” said Anneliese Midgley, the Labour government’s newest head of party discipline, shedding some light on her direct approach to keeping MPs in line.

Midgley, the MP for Knowsley, who is one of the prime minister’s closest friends in government, has surprised some Labour MPs with her strikingly “frank yet glam” interview in Vogue in which she said she was determined to win. She also highlighted her unlikely journey from a deprived Liverpool housing estate via the arts world to the heart of government.

But it was her honesty in regards to being tough that caught attention from her Labour colleagues who hoped Burnham’s reign would be marked by an end to Keir Starmer’s strict party management style.

Burnham wrote to MPs back in July: “I want to create a different culture where MPs are happy and fulfilled doing their jobs, where everyone has a part to play and where opinions and approaches are respected, even where there’s difference … the whips’ office should be our HR department, not something to be feared or where discipline is used to stifle debate.”

At the time many Labour MPs, particularly those on the party’s left wing, breathed a sigh of relief – until he appointed Midgley as his chief whip, with some even going as far as saying they would be in “her bad books” because “I’m not one of her buddies she hangs and drinks with on the parliamentary terrace”.

Midgley, who worked as Jeremy Corbyn’s deputy chief of staff and Starmer’s senior special adviser, criticised the former prime minister’s approach to managing the parliamentary Labour party (PLP) and praised Burnham’s approach – a man she said she “would run through the walls for”.

On party discipline, Midgley said: “These are grown-ups who should be treated with absolute respect, who’ve got a wealth of ideas and advice – not just treated as a number to go through a voting lobby.”

When challenged on whether she thought Starmer had treated MPs “as a number”, the chief whip replied: “Yeah, I do think that.”

Despite her celebration of Burnham’s collegiate approach, Midgley told the magazine: “I’m very determined. If there’s things I want to do, I will do them. Basically, I will win,” she said, laughing, according to the magazine.

“Obviously, I said all of that stuff before about team-building, and that’s absolutely right. But like, I’m not going to take any shit and I don’t fuck about. Do you know what I mean?”

One MP described the interview as striking, not just because chief whips usually keep their heads down and far away from the spotlight, but because Midgley managed to articulate herself as an MP bringing a new era into the “dark arts” of “chief whipping”, being one that has artistic taste, fashion sense and the determination to rise from child poverty to being an influential minister.

The interview appeared to mark another way in which Burnham’s government was attempting to start a new phase in Labour politics, or simply making itself appear more human, while “scaring the shit out of the PLP”, according to one senior Labour MP.

title: Police launch investigation into David Walliams over alleged serious sexual offences
excerpt:
Met police say allegations are separate from those made by multiple women in Guardian and ITV investigation

The Metropolitan police have launched a criminal investigation into David Walliams over all...
body_text:
Met police say allegations are separate from those made by multiple women in Guardian and ITV investigation

The Metropolitan police have launched a criminal investigation into David Walliams over alleged serious sexual offences.

Walliams, 55, was accused in reports by ITV and the Guardian this week of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex. He has denied any wrongdoing, being a sexual predator or breaking the law.

The Met said the allegations it was investigating were separate to those reported by the Guardian and ITV but as “part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences”.

The new allegations made to police are understood to have come from several people. Some date back to the 2000s and are described by police as “non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s”.

It is understood at least some of those who made reports to the police did so this week and had given initial accounts to detectives from the Met’s specialist crime division. Those accounts were enough for the Met to launch a full criminal investigation by detectives specialising in serious and complex sexual offences.

Police declined to detail the alleged offences, or where and when they are alleged to have occurred, saying this was to minimise the chances of the people who had complained being identified. Detectives stressed that those making the allegations were entitled to life-long anonymity.

It is police policy not to name people under investigation, and in a statement announcing the criminal investigation, the force said: “In recent days, the Met has received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s.

“Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers.

“The allegations are separate from those reported by ITN and the Guardian. However, as part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences.”

The Guardian and ITV News reported the allegations against Walliams after a court rejected a legal attempt aimed at preventing publication. Walliams has not been arrested and is in a medical facility.

Det Supt Mike Cagney, from the Met’s complex sexual offences unit which is leading the investigation, said: “We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.

“We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process.”

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the media investigation, Walliams wrote: “Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

“I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.”

He added: “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.”

Police have not carried out any searches as part of their investigation and one of their central aims is to support and keep the confidence of those who have complained to them about being victims of sexual offending.

The allegations made to the Guardian include accounts from two women who said they first met Walliams when they were 15 years old. Both women, now in their 30s, said they felt they had been groomed by him two decades ago, and that the experience had continued to affect them.

Walliams was accused of abusing his position to pursue women through the family television show Britain’s Got Talent and at his former children’s book publisher, HarperCollins, where he is alleged to have had a sexual relationship with a junior member of staff.

The allegations were revealed in a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News that heard from 30 sources with first-hand accounts of his conduct.

Since the allegations were published, Walliams has been dropped by his literary agency, the BBC has begun to remove his programmes from iPlayer and the Labour party has suspended his membership.

The Met said people could report information to police by calling 101 and providing the reference 4900/10NOV26, or by contacting the complex sexual offences unit on 0207 175 2738.

title: Video from inside Brooklyn apartment captures moment New York City building collapsed, killing 8
excerpt:
Video from inside an apartment showed when the building next door in New York City collapsed Wednesday. (Credit: Anderson Velez)

Newly released video from inside a Brooklyn apartment captures the ter...
body_text:
Video from inside an apartment showed when the building next door in New York City collapsed Wednesday. (Credit: Anderson Velez)

Newly released video from inside a Brooklyn apartment captures the terrifying moment the building collapsed earlier this week, killing eight people and injuring nearly 20 others.

The three-story structure in Flatbush caved in on Wednesday, prompting a massive emergency response.

Recorded inside the third-floor unit of resident Anderson Velez, video shows the apartment beginning to give way just as a living room wall crumbles.

AT LEAST 2 DEAD, 17 INJURED AFTER NYC BUILDING COLLAPSE

First responders work the scene after a building collapsed in the Brooklyn borough of New York on Wednesday, killing eight people. (Ryan Murphy/AP Photo)

According to Gothamist, Velez’s 9-year-old son can be seen holding a baby bottle and pulling a gallon of milk from the refrigerator while a 2-year-old plays nearby. Moments later, Velez's wife bursts through a doorway screaming, and the boy runs toward his mother as the walls break apart around them.

"I am still in shock," Velez told the news outlet. "The truth is, I’m trying to be strong for my son, but I feel terrible."

BODIES OF TWO IRON WORKERS RECOVERED FROM RUBBLE OF PHILADELPHIA PARKING GARAGE 5 DAYS AFTER PARTIAL COLLAPSE

Rescue crews spent hours sifting through the rubble before confirming the eight fatalities.

"I am heartbroken that eight New Yorkers have now lost their lives and at least 17 have been injured, including three firefighters," New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote on X.

WORKERS WARNED OHIO TRENCH WAS TOO DEEP BUT WERE TOLD TO ENTER MINUTES BEFORE FATAL CAVE-IN: REPORT

An excavator pulls rubble away from the site where a building collapsed in Brooklyn on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. (James Cirrone for Fox News Digital)

"There are no words for a loss of this magnitude," he added. "My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we have lost, those who are injured and everyone grieving today."

Meanwhile, the owner of the neighboring property is facing scrutiny over past construction violations — including a contractor’s decision to ignore a city stop-work order in March, Fox News Digital previously reported.

CONSTRUCTION RIG COLLAPSES ON 3 CARS IN MIAMI, TRAPS WORKERS AS FIRE ERUPTS

New York City Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani confirmed that excavation was underway at the adjacent Bedford Avenue site at the time of the collapse.

"The type of work they were conducting was excavation work on that job site. And so, that was what they were working on today," Tigani said.

MANHATTAN BUILDING DEVELOPER SAYS COLLAPSE FEARS WERE OVERBLOWN, CALLS BUCKLING COLUMNS 'LOCALIZED SITUATION'

First responders tend to a collapsed building in Brooklyn in New York on Nov. 11, 2026. (kena betancur/AFP via Getty Images)

"They have a plan approved for a three-story building, but they have current plans looking for a nine-story building, which has not yet been approved for," Tigani added. "At this point, all we have at this time is excavation work in that section of the construction site."

Fox News Digital's Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Russia strikes hospital in central Kyiv after SpaceX system falters again
excerpt:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says speed restrictions on Starshield system made it harder for Ukraine to shoot down drones

Russia has attacked a hospital in the centre of Kyiv, close to several western embassi...
body_text:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says speed restrictions on Starshield system made it harder for Ukraine to shoot down drones

Russia has attacked a hospital in the centre of Kyiv, close to several western embassies, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said speed restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield system had made it harder for Ukraine to shoot down enemy drones.

Three people were injured when a drone smashed into the National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedics at 3am, hitting the second floor of the hospital and an adjoining 19th-century building.

Meanwhile, Russia claimed it had shot down nearly 1,200 Ukrainian drones overnight, one of the largest swarms sent by Kyiv. It reported that at least four people were killed in the southern region of Volgograd.

The blast in Kyiv blew out windows in nearby buildings including in the National Academy of Arts across the road. The six-storey hospital is located in the Shevchenkivskyi district, not far from the Danish and Romanian embassies, as well as cafes and a park popular with dog walkers.

Standing in the yard as smoke billowed from the burning building, and firefighters led dazed patients to safety, one witness, Oleksandr, said the attack had narrowly missed patients. “We were asleep when there was this massive boom. We all jumped out of bed straight away.

“There was glass all over the floor. People were running about … If it had hit a little further to the left it would have been much worse. We felt the shock wave.”

He added: “Targeting the wounded – that’s really low. Russia attacks everything. Where I live, high-rise blocks are being constantly hit by bombs. They don’t care where they drop them, or where they land.”

Russia has recently stepped up its strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, hitting power plants, passenger trains and two bridges across the Dnipro river. Ukraine says the attacks are part of a campaign of terror, designed to make a weary population capitulate.

On Thursday, Zelenskyy said the Starshield system – operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and overseen by the Pentagon – was again experiencing significant disruptions, after an unexplained slowdown last month.

He said some Russian aerial sorties had got through because Ukrainian interceptor systems that rely on the US satellite service could not reach the necessary speed to knock out enemy drones. Starshield is the Ukrainian military’s version of Starlink.

The White House has yet to explain why the service has been throttled for a second time, but it comes after intense US-led shuttle diplomacy this week, with Donald Trump seemingly pressuring Zelenskyy to make territorial concessions to Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.

Trump’s emissaries, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and real estate developer Steve Witkoff, met Putin in Moscow on Thursday. They then flew to Dublin to brief Zelenskyy on their talks, which came after trilateral negotiations on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi.

Kremlin negotiators insist that Ukraine hand over four Ukrainian provinces, including cities and villages Russian troops have been unable to conquer. They are also calling for a new “security architecture” in Europe – a demand in effect that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture, before eastern European nations joined the alliance.

At the same time, Moscow does not want European states to be involved in US-brokered talks to end the war in Ukraine. On Thursday, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, said Europe had to take part since “US support” for Kyiv had ended.

“Without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine,” Macron said. “At the end of the day, we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans.”

Meanwhile, Russian strikes ⁠on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ⁠overnight caused ⁠power ​outages in 12 ⁠regions, said deputy energy minister Artem ⁠Nekrasov. The ‌affected regions are ‌Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Zhytomyr, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Rivne, Sumy, Kharkiv, ‌Khmelnytskyi and Chernihiv.

“Energy workers ​are working at an intensified pace, ⁠but new attacks ​and constant ​air raid ​alerts ​are ‌complicating and delaying ​repairs,” ​Nekrasov said.

In Kyiv, the orthopaedic hospital’s director, Ronan Derkach, said medical services had been temporarily suspended as a cleanup operation got under way. Thirty patients were taken to safety.

title: Iranophobia: Netanyahu’s bid to transform fear into political survival
excerpt: As the right-wing coalition government that oversaw the genocide in Gaza, launched attacks across the region, and eroded civil liberties at home appears to lose its grip on power by the day, caretaker...
body_text:
As the right-wing coalition government that oversaw the genocide in Gaza, launched attacks across the region, and eroded civil liberties at home appears to lose its grip on power by the day, caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s increasingly frantic efforts to derail the political transition suggest a growing desperation to stay in office.

Among those efforts appears to be an attempt to reignite the war with Iran. Netanyahu has reportedly ordered the Israeli military to prepare for war ahead of a potential attack on Iran, in defiance of the opposition’s calls for restraint.

The reports follow revelations that Netanyahu had been phoning US President Donald Trump almost daily to press for renewed strikes on Iran. Israeli media have also reported repeated confrontations between Netanyahu and military chief Eyal Zamir, who has resisted proposals for military action against Iran, warning that they could trigger a wider conflict.

Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been tasked with forming a viable government, but that is not a foregone conclusion. Netanyahu has been pushing for a national unity government that would include himself and his Likud party, or waiting for Eisenkot to fail, leading to another election.

“Netanyahu is desperate,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli political analyst at King’s College London, said. “He knows – and you can see it from his behaviour – that it is likely that he is politically done, and only a national unity government could save him.”

“A little war could compel Eisenkot & Co,” he said, referring to the opposition bloc and its leader, Gadi Eisenkot, “to form such a government in a time of crisis.”

Many in the opposition, including Eisenkot himself, have accused Netanyahu of attempting to drag the country into a potentially devastating war for his own political survival, or of deliberately stalling the coalition-building process in the hope of running down the clock and forcing another election.

Yet while critics see Netanyahu’s attempts to reignite war with Iran as a cynical bid to retain power, analysts have suggested that even his fiercest opponents could rally behind him if he does launch an attack.

“It’s paradoxical,” said Haggai Ram, a professor at Ben-Gurion University and author of the book Iranophobia, which details Israel’s longstanding hostility to Tehran. “Everyone knows it would be contrived, but the hysteria over Iran cuts through everything. If Netanyahu succeeds, and manages to start a war with Iran, of course the opposition would fall in behind him, and the public would expect them to. They’d recognise the cynicism for what it was, but this is Iran. This is the great enemy.”

“For the former military members of the opposition, confronting Iran was what they spent their entire lives training for. For the public, after years of being told of the Iranian threat, many already see the war as inevitable,” he said.

Israel’s decades-long cold war with Iran has been a constant throughout much of the Israeli population’s lifetime. For decades, Israelis have lived with the threat of attacks from Iran’s regional allies, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, whose rhetoric threatening Israel’s destruction has been widely reported in Israeli media.

That fear has been reinforced by repeated warnings from Israeli leaders, dating back to at least the 1990s, that Tehran was on the brink of acquiring a nuclear weapon and would likely use it against Israel.

Tensions came to a head as Israel launched multiple wars across the region following the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023. A 12-day exchange of strikes with Iran in June 2025 was followed by a joint attack with the US launched in February, which has disrupted some of the world’s critical waterways, thrown financial markets into turmoil, and affected household expenditure across much of the world.

Nevertheless, another war with Iran may offer Netanyahu a route out of the political bind he finds himself in, political psychologist Daniel Bar-Tal of Tel Aviv University suggested.

As things stand, a majority of the public oppose him and his coalition, and, in Bar-Tal’s framing, he is “fighting for his life”, with multiple active criminal cases against him.

Although Bar-Tal doubted that Trump, Israel’s principal ally and military backer, would allow Netanyahu to derail US negotiations with Iran, he believed that Israelis would still “support such a war, and this is a good card for him to play [to create the] turmoil” needed to extricate himself from his current predicament.

For now, Ram said, Israel maintains what, for many, feels like a state of permanent expectation.

“People know that any case for war would be manufactured,” he said. “They’re not stupid and they see it for what it is. However, many people – including some of my friends and students – regard it as inevitable. They’re just waiting, and if and when it happens, despite everything they know, they will still report for duty and do what they’re ordered.”

title: Which NFL teams can actually win the Super Bowl? Ranking all 32 at the season’s halfway point
excerpt:
Tom Brady lists his top 10 teams for Week 9 which include the Chicago Bears, San Francisco 49ers, Kansas City Chiefs and more!

The NFL hit the halfway mark after Week 9, so it seems like a good time ...
body_text:
Tom Brady lists his top 10 teams for Week 9 which include the Chicago Bears, San Francisco 49ers, Kansas City Chiefs and more!

The NFL hit the halfway mark after Week 9, so it seems like a good time to ask how many teams can actually win the Super Bowl.

The answer (spoiler alert) isn’t 32. I’m not sure it’s even 10.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

NFL WEEK 9 SUNDAY TAKEAWAYS: BENGALS, 49ERS AND PACKERS LOOK SUPER, RAMS FINALLY OVER .500

Let’s start with the legitimate contenders and work our way down to the teams that don’t have a snowball’s chance in hell.

If I’m picking a team to win the Super Bowl today, give me Buffalo. The Bills lead the NFL at 32 points per game, and four of their final nine games are against the Jets and Dolphins, who have three wins between them. That’s a pretty good spot for a team that already holds the AFC’s No. 1 seed.

Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills are at the top of the list of potential Super Bowl contenders. (Getty Images)

Josh Allen has played in two AFC Championship Games, both at Arrowhead. If Buffalo keeps the top seed, the Bills get a first-round bye and need two home wins to reach the Super Bowl. I’ll take my chances with Allen in Buffalo twice.

I called San Francisco the best team in the NFL after Week 4, and the 49ers are still my pick to come out of the NFC. Ricky Pearsall went down before the season started, Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel have both missed time, and Christian Kirk is back on injured reserve. Through all of that, Brock Purdy has completed 69% of his passes and thrown 17 touchdowns against five interceptions.

Now the 49ers have added Keenan Allen. If Evans and Samuel get healthy, good luck getting this offense off the field in January.

The only part of the Jets game that made me reconsider Kansas City’s Super Bowl chances was when Patrick Mahomes hurt his arm. He came back on the next possession, and the Chiefs went on to win by 23. Kansas City has allowed 143 points in eight games, so Mahomes has a defense that can buy him time when the offense starts slowly. If he’s healthy in January and gets the ball with a chance to end your season, how good do you feel about your chances?

Joe Burrow is my MVP at the halfway point. He brought the Bengals back from 13 down in back-to-back games, including an overtime win against Tennessee. I’d prefer they quit making him do that. Spotting the Titans 13 is one thing. Try doing it in Buffalo in January.

The defense held Atlanta to 17 points in Spain. If that group can play like that more often, Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins can win the whole thing.

Yeah, I called the Packers bad after they barely beat Tampa Bay in Week 4 (whoops). Green Bay has gone 5-1 since the loss to Atlanta, and the one loss in that stretch was a game I thought they should have won in Detroit. Then they put up 45 against New England and picked off Drake Maye three times. If both sides of the ball are going to play like that, the Packers can win the NFC. The games against Minnesota and the Rams should tell us whether I’m about to change my mind again.

Jordan Love and the Green Bay Packers made my September assessment of their team look pretty silly. (Getty Images)

The Rams are the team in this group I’d be least surprised to see miss the playoffs. Three weeks ago, they were 2-4 and Arizona was spending most of the afternoon in Matthew Stafford’s lap. Now they’ve won three straight and Myles Garrett is back.

Sean McVay just needs to scrape out enough wins to get in while Puka Nacua and Davante Adams heal. The offensive line still worries me, but if both receivers are healthy in January and the Rams can keep Stafford upright, I’d hate to be the division winner that draws them in the first round.

Ben Johnson won games with Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent, so I’m sold on the coaching. Caleb Williams is the reason I can see Chicago winning it all and the reason I’m keeping the Bears here. He threw two touchdowns on his first 16 attempts against Tampa Bay and four interceptions on his next 16. Williams has tantalizing physical gifts and is arguably the most talented player in the NFL right now. But mistakes are amplified in the playoffs and Williams still makes a few too many for me to have Chicago in the same tier as the teams above.

Trevor Lawrence is playing some of the best football of his career, and Jacksonville has outscored its opponents by 108 points. I get why people are higher on the Jaguars than I am. I also watched them commit 13 penalties while nearly giving away a win in Cincinnati, then let C.J. Stroud throw for 312 yards and three touchdowns in London. I can see the Jaguars winning the division and a home playoff game. But the AFC is loaded at the top and to me, the Jags are a notch below the Bills, Bengals and Chiefs.

I had Seattle in the Super Bowl conversation when it played San Francisco in Week 5, and the defense that held Kansas City to three points is a good reason to keep the Seahawks there. A week after that Chiefs game, Seattle gave up 34 to Chicago. Shutting down Gardner Minshew and the Cardinals didn’t settle much for me. I’m more interested in what the defending champs look like when they get another crack at the 49ers on Nov. 29.

Seattle Seahawks head coach Mike MacDonald has had to deal with multiple injuries to quarterback Sam Darnold, but if he can het his team healthy, they can still make a run in the NFC. (AP Photo/Phelan M. Ebenhack)

Detroit has won four straight, and I trust Jared Goff and Jahmyr Gibbs to score against just about anyone. The defense is why I have the Lions in this tier. Holding Jordan Love and the Packers to 17 points carries the most weight with me, and even in that game, Green Bay missed a 35-yard field goal that would’ve given it the lead late.

The other three wins came against Jacoby Brissett, Kyler Murray and Malik Willis. I’ll feel better about Detroit’s chances in January if that defense can hold up against Caleb Williams and the Bears on Thanksgiving.

Seven wins and a plus-12 point differential feels about right for the Broncos I’ve watched. They nearly lost to the winless Chargers and got the better end of some questionable calls against Carolina, a game they still needed a Nik Bonitto strip-sack to finish. And it wasn’t the first time this season that Denver needed some help from the officials to win a game. If you’ve read me for any length of time, you know I don’t believe in Sean Payton or Bo Nix. But mostly Sean Payton, the NFL’s most overrated head coach.

I think Kevin O’Connell is one of the best coaches in the NFL, and he deserves plenty of credit for getting the Vikings to 6-2. I also questioned what to make of their 5-0 start when their previous three opponents had a combined 2-13 record. Then Minnesota scored six points against Buffalo on Monday Night Football. O’Connell can scheme his way to a lot of wins, but I’m skeptical he can get enough from the quarterback position to survive the tough NFC, even after trading for quarterback Kirk Cousins.

Remember when I wondered if Drake Maye was a one-hit wonder? He promptly went into Buffalo and won, then accounted for five touchdowns against the Raiders. The Patriots have already beaten my No. 1 team on the road, so I know what their best looks like. I also know what it looked like when Maye threw three picks against Green Bay. I’d need to see a longer stretch of the Buffalo version before I buy a return trip to the Super Bowl.

DRAKE MAYE TELLS REPORTERS THEY DON'T KNOW 'WHAT THEY'RE TALKING ABOUT' DURING GERMANY PRESS CONFERENCE

I thought Aaron Rodgers was cooked, and he responded by throwing nine touchdowns in three games. The Steelers have already beaten Cincinnati, and I can see Rodgers winning a home playoff game at 43. Now picture Pittsburgh having to win a shootout against Joe Burrow one week and going on the road to face Josh Allen or Patrick Mahomes the next. I just don't see a February run out of this team.

John Harbaugh has the Giants in first place despite losing Jaxson Dart and having to shuffle quarterbacks. That’s a good coaching job. The reward for winning the NFC East is a likely home playoff game against a wild-card team from the NFC North or West that’s considerably better than the Giants.

Five wins are more than I expected after watching Deshaun Watson in Week 1. And Week 2. And Week 3. You get it. The Browns are winning despite subpar quarterback play, not because their signal callers have done a good job. Eventually, that poor play is going to lead to a lot more losses.

The Cleveland Browns haven't gotten great quarterback play out of Deshaun Watson or Shedeur Sanders this season. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

I was giving Jesse Minter some early Coach of the Year credit after he took Tyler Huntley into Atlanta and won. That was four losses ago. And with Lamar Jackson expected to be out for 6-to-9 weeks, this season is basically over.

I thought the Raiders were better than people expected, and they were competitive against both Kansas City and Buffalo. They’ve also gone 1-5 since starting 3-0, and the 49ers just beat them by three touchdowns. The Raiders themselves seemingly gave up on the season by trading Kirk Cousins and handing the offense to No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza. I’m looking forward to seeing what the kid can do, but the future is not now.

Every year, we’re're told "this is the year" for the Dallas Cowboys and every year ... it isn't. This season is no exception. The Cowboys just racked up 153 penalty yards and needed a last-minute touchdown to beat the Colts. The NFC East is still within reach, which says more about the NFC East than it does about Dallas. Even if they sneak into the playoffs, they aren’t going to make a Super Bowl run.

Houston has won three of its last four games after starting 0-4. C.J. Stroud threw for 312 yards and three touchdowns in an impressive win over Jacksonville in London. A week later, the Texans lost at home to the Giants in overtime. The Texans dug themselves a pretty big hole, and while I think they're one of the better teams in this tier, they're just too inconsistent to be considered a real contender.

It’s actually fascinating to see the Panthers here, right below the Texans. Following their rookie seasons, everyone thought C.J. Stroud was a can't-miss star and Bryce Young was a bust. The truth is that both are competent, but not spectacular, NFL starters. I’m more impressed by Young, since he easily could have let his career go down the tubes after a terrible start, but he showed some heart and grit to battle back. Unfortunately, there’s just not enough talent around him in Carolina right now.

Tyler Shough and Chris Olave have made the Saints more fun to watch than I expected. Shough threw for 410 yards and came a two-point conversion from beating Detroit, then beat Baltimore the next week. There’s something to build around here, and the NFC South gives them a chance to make things interesting this year. But the winner of the NFC South, like the winner of the NFC East, is likely to be a one-and-done playoff team.

Tyler Shough and the New Orleans Saints have some exciting young pieces, but they aren't ready to compete for a Super Bowl at this point. (Getty Images)

The Bucs did well to get back into the division race after starting 0-4. Then they picked off Caleb Williams four times, scored three points off those interceptions and lost. It was a bit of a microcosm of the entire NFC South, which is filled with teams that just aren’t that good and can even lose games when seemingly everything goes right.

Like every team in the NFC South, the Falcons are still very much in the picture. The problem is that they aren't very good and their next three games are against the Chiefs, Vikings and Lions. This team needs to figure out if Michael Penix is the answer and, if not, start making plans to replace him in the 2027 NFL Draft.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

I’m still a Jayden Daniels truther. I also watched Washington get into field-goal range in overtime against the Giants and let the clock run out without trying a kick. Dan Quinn seems like a good dude who his players really like, but he’s just not a good enough head coach. Daniels needs one of those young offensive gurus who can unlock his full potential.

Arizona Cardinals (3-6), Indianapolis Colts (2-7), New York Jets (2-7), Philadelphia Eagles (2-7), Miami Dolphins (1-7), Tennessee Titans (1-7), Los Angeles Chargers (0-8)

If you root for one of these teams, I hope you like mock drafts (lucky for you, I write several mock drafts every year!). I talked myself into the Jets in September (whoops), and Arizona can still spring an upset every now and then.

The Titans’ only win came against the Colts. Philadelphia has lost seven straight, Miami fans have been looking toward April since September, and the Chargers have Justin Herbert and still haven’t won a game.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

A few of these teams could spend the offseason looking for a head coach, a quarterback or both. I wouldn’t be surprised if some of these fan bases are pulling up mock drafts again next November.

title: Man charged after seven women sexually assaulted in 30 minutes on UK campus
excerpt:
Police called to Huddersfield University on Tuesday after women reported being ‘approached and grabbed’

A 29-year-old man has been charged after seven women reported being sexually assaulted on the H...
body_text:
Police called to Huddersfield University on Tuesday after women reported being ‘approached and grabbed’

A 29-year-old man has been charged after seven women reported being sexually assaulted on the Huddersfield University campus over a 30 minute period.

West Yorkshire police said Sophan Akbash had been charged with nine counts of sexual assault and would appear at Leeds magistrates court on Friday. Security staff called officers to Huddersfield University on Tuesday evening after reports of a man approaching and sexually touching women on and near the campus, police said.

Officers said seven women had been sexually assaulted by a suspect between 6 and 6.30pm on Tuesday. The women “had made off” from a suspect “after he approached and grabbed at them”, police added.

On Friday, the force confirmed that Akbash, of Huddersfield, had been charged with nine counts of sexual assault.

Earlier this week, Det Insp Sarah Bradley of West Yorkshire police said: “We continue to work closely with our partners at the university to provide reassurance to students and staff, and remain fully committed to supporting victims and safeguarding those who live, study and work in Huddersfield.”

The university’s deputy vice-chancellor, Prof Tim Thornton, said on Wednesday: “We recognise that incidents of this nature are deeply concerning and we are providing wellbeing support to anyone affected.

“As a precaution, we have increased security patrols around campus and are encouraging all members of our community to make use of our SafeZone app, which provides direct access to emergency assistance, wellbeing support and our campus support and safety team. We remain committed to maintaining a safe and supportive environment for everyone who studies, works and visits our campus.”

title: Leaders meet in Dublin amid search for lead EU negotiator for peace talks with Russia - Europe live
excerpt:
Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand next round of negotiations to include European countries

Fun aside, the host camera captured an interesting exchange between Ireland and Denmark’s Frederiksen...
body_text:
Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand next round of negotiations to include European countries

Fun aside, the host camera captured an interesting exchange between Ireland and Denmark’s Frederiksen, with the Danish PM stressing to the Irish leader the importance of agreeing on a winter support package for Ukraine.

She said more help was needed to “get them through a tough, tough winter.”

“So if everybody could put something on the table, that would be very welcome,” she said.

Some other fun nuggets from the doorstep (10:53) include Croatia’s Andrej Plenković joking that Ireland’s Martin “is always here” rooted in the same spot where he welcomes the leaders.

Meanwhile, Poland’s Donald Tusk got a cheerful “dzień dobry” – good morning in Polish – from the official leading him through the building.

And if you’re wondering what the leaders are talking about between themselves on the doorstep, then I’m afraid the answer is very boring: it’s mostly the weather.

Several other leaders also remarked on how beautiful Dublin looks in the morning sun, with their arrival handler joking: “it’s always like that in Dublin in November… almost.”

The only two who had any, let’s say, doubts about the weather were, unsurprisingly, two southern leaders: Cyprus’s Nikos Christodoulides and Greece’s Kyriakos Mitsotakis.

In contrast, Germany’s Friedrich Merz, Finland’s Petteri Orpo, Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson, Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen and Austria’s Christian Stocker even opted for a nice stroll to the venue together.

This caused a bit of a diplomatic protocol challenge in terms of who should go through the door to see Ireland’s Micheál Martin first, with everyone stuck in an awkward cycle of pointing and “oh, please” until Merz eventually suggested Frederiksen go first, suggesting “ladies first.”

“Lady first,” she said, with a bit of a side eye, and stepped ahead.

Either way, the doors to the meeting room are now closed, and the discussions under way.

Meanwhile, Latvian PM Andris Kulbergs has a strong entry for the quote of the day competition, as he said “we, as Europe, have to grow some bigger balls.”

“I think we as Europe have to grow some bigger balls, because we are bigger in size, … in military might, in all the economic aspects.

Look where is Russia: Russia is not capable of even taking such an, in size, in population, smaller power as Ukraine, which is showing a great, great spirit and fighting back [for the] fifth year.

And Russia is [now] raising points that we have no accept? Sorry, that’s the aggressor, losing on the frontline. We should be raising our expectations, what has to be done in terms of Ukraine’s security.”

Hungary’s Péter Magyar is also here, looking very elegant as always…

… but it looks like he took a slight detour on the way back to hotel last night to try and pour a perfect pint of Guinness.

Luxembourg’s PM Luc Frieden is in a slightly unusual position this morning as he is representing as many as three countries at today’s meeting in Dublin.

Belgian and Dutch PMs have skipped the summit as they face political problems at home, leaving Frieden with three hats and representing not his usual 690,000 people, but some 30 million people today.

“We had a meeting of the Benelux prime ministers two days ago in Maastricht. And so I know that when I speak here on their behalf, that on the fundamental issues that are being discussed here today – Ukraine, AI – we are very much aligned.”

He says he has got “some of their speaking points” from Belgium and the Netherlands to help him get through the meeting today.

He stressed that the three Benelux countries “are on the side of Ukraine,” and that “there is need for solidarity of all 27 member states” on further financial support for Kyiv.

On who should represent the EU in any future talks, he said “we cannot let neither the Americans nor the Russians decide about our future,” and suggested EU’s Costa “has an important role to play.”

There’s also a bit of national news on the side, with Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson confirming he will send his proposal to the Swedish Centre party later today in the latest bid to break the deadlock and form a new government, more than 60 days after the election.

The party – which could decide the shape of the next government – has asked the leaders of the centre-left Social Democrats and centre-right Moderates to share their proposals on how they could work together in office.

The deadline expires this afternoon, and hopefully the exercise will get us a bit closer to resolving the current standoff.

Both offers have their problems: the more natural, centre-left grouping, led by S’s Magdalena Andersson, is paralysed by the Left’s demand for cabinet decisions – a move the Centre party has said would be unacceptable.

But the alternative, led by Kristersson, would equally pose awkward questions for the Centre Party vis a vis the far-right Sweden Democrats – although the party offered they could remain in opposition, but support a minority centre-right government.

Kristersson sought to strike a conciliatory tone in Dublin, as he courted the centrists:

“I recognise that the Centre Party is under immense pressure right now – at times, the rhetoric has been quite harsh, bordering on insulting. I have no intention of engaging in that; instead, I respect the Centre Party’s right to choose its own path.”

“I do not intend to go into the details of the proposals we are presenting to the Centre Party; these are intended for their own internal deliberations.

However, I can say that this is a policy reform agenda representing a centrist, center-right political approach.”

On Ukraine, Kristersson said “what Russia does speaks volumes more than anything Russia might say during various negotiations,” saying he does not have “high hopes” about the current talks – but they still were worth pursuing.

He said the discussion on who should represent Europe is “slightly overstated,” as the focus should be on Europe’s interests, not personalities.

He said that some of the issues are “pure EU interests” to be represented by EU institutions, but others should involve the largest countries, including also the UK.

“I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has warned against the EU agreeing to Russia’s proposed sequence of talks on Ukraine, saying it would allow Moscow to “divert the attention away” from its actions and ultimately leave Europe “in a worse place.”

She welcomed the US side “finally admitting what I said already one and a half years ago – that for any deal between Russia and Ukraine … you also need the Europeans.”

“I hope that we are just not at the table, but we are actually also really influencing the outcome of these negotiations.”

“The most important is that we keep to our agreement that first the ceasefire, then peace agreement and then any kind of other talks … when Russia is still presenting their maximum demands, then we should also stick to the maximum demands and start to negotiate from there. …

Kallas warned that there is a risk of Europeans “actually walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as Moscow is trying to “divert the attention away from that there is no ceasefire and actually [get us to] start to listen to their claims.”

“If we walk into that trap that we start to discuss … the European security architecture, then I don’t think we are in a better place. We are actually in worse place.”

“Let’s focus on what it is at hand. We have one aggressor and one victim. The aggressor does not have security concerns, as nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”

Kallas is also very clear that she wants to be part of the EU negotiating team, saying she was appointed to represent Europe on foreign and security policy.

“I know that the Russians don’t want me, but do we have a say on who is representing Russia? No, we don’t.”

She also said that ultimately she would not be “representing myself,” but bound by any mandate given to her by the 27.

Slightly amused/frustrated with repeated questions on what’s holding up the EU with deciding on its representation, she eventually hits back with this line:

“Well, we have institutions in place, so we can’t just send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending. Clearly, we should not copy the same patterns.”

Asked why she thinks the Russians do not want her to be involved in the negotiations, she says:

“They don’t want [anyone] strong on the other side because they want to push their through their maximum demands, like they have always done. Because … their tactics is very clear: at first you present threats and ultimatums, you use force, and then you will just wait, because there will always be people in the west who will offer you something you didn’t have before. And every time you go further.

So, of course, if you negotiate with anybody, you want the other side to be as weak as possible so that you can get what you want.”

It’s a pretty chilly morning in Dublin, but the European Council president, António Costa, is keen to signal to his hosts that he’s ready to do business, showing off a cute Irish green scarf to Ireland’s Micheál Martin.

Today’s host, Ireland’s Micheál Martin, said discussions will focus on what Europe needs to consider any future Ukraine settlement a just and sustainable peace.

“The substance of any peace agreement is as important as who represents Europe. Europe needs to be very clear in terms of what would constitute a sustainable peace for the continent, well into the future. Security guarantees are a significant part of that, and also the reconstruction of Ukraine.”

He said the outstanding questions on Europe’s priorities and representation need to be decided “in the next week or two.”

On AI, he said the meeting will “explore the implications of AI, positive … plus the potential negatives, and the balance between regulation and innovation.”

Estonian prime minister Kristen Michal has warned that Ukraine faces “winter … like hell again,” with Russia “bombing everything” as he urged European leaders to double down on their backing for Kyiv.

“Putin has to change his goals because the war, aggression, and killing of women, children, and civilians would stop right now if he gave an order.”

“The European plan for a while [has been] quite simple: help Ukraine push Russia and so should it be.”

Michal warned that Putin’s attempt to discuss the broader European security architecture before agreeing to end the war is “a mental trap” by Russia’s Putin.

“Does anybody really think that Europe is a threat to Russia? This is not sane talk to be honest.

So, I would say that our red line is quite clear: we should have peace, on Ukraine’s terms, and after that everything can be talked, but not before and not at the same time.”

The Estonian PM also said that if the EU needs to send its negotiators, the European Council president António Costa and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas are “the persons to do it”.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen insisted it is “self-explanatory” that Europe should be included in the peace talks on Ukraine “to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine.”

“We will come forward as a commission with a proposal for the financing of the Ukrainian needs in 2027, and with the 22nd sanctions package before the next European Council,” she said.

von der Leyen also said today’s talks would focus on “the risks … but also the opportunities’ associated with the rise of AI.

EU leaders will continue talks on their diplomatic and financial support for Ukraine today, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged them to “pay attention” to Vladimir Putin’s demands on security.

European leaders meeting in Dublin on Thursday rejected calls that there was any need to recreate a European security architecture, while restating that Russia needed to stop attacking Ukraine.

European Council president António Costa summed it up:

“There is no need to reinvent the wheel. Europe had a functioning European security architecture until it was first, gradually undermined, and ultimately destroyed by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.”

Speaking to reporters the UK prime minister Andy Burnham said Europe “in the wider sense” i.e not just the EU, would decide on its own arrangements.

“In terms of the wider point, there was a very strong feeling that you know, Russian demands to put the question of European security architecture or European security arrangements into this negotiation – that is not up for negotiation... It is for Europe to decide its own arrangements. Europe and Europe alone. And again, I am talking in the wider sense when I say that.”

Around 40 countries, most of the attendees of the European Political Community summit on Thursday, signed a declaration drafted by France declaring that European states “bear a primary responsibility and are assuming greater responsibility for the security of Europe”.

EU leaders are continuing talks in Dublin on Friday, focusing on AI. But following interventions from Giorgia Meloni and Friedrich Merz, they will also discuss Europe’s role in international peace talks and the question of future financial support for Ukraine.

EU leaders are meeting in Dublin today for discussions on Ukraine and AI, among others, as they continue their search for a lead EU negotiator in any peace talks with Russia.

Their discussions are becoming increasingly urgent, after Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include European countries, US envoy Jared Kushner said last night after meeting Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin.

“This will allow us to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Kushner ​said ​later on X.

But, as he somewhat mockingly said on Wednesday,

“If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations.”

Let’s see what comes out of these discussions, with the leaders also expected to talk about AI.

Elsewhere, I am still keeping an eye on the Dutch government crisis as Rob Jetten works hard to avoid the collapse of his minority cabinet.

It’s Friday, 13 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

title: Van Hollen takes aim at Schumer as Democrats face first big test after midterms – US politics live
excerpt:
Senator Van Hollen says midterm results show Americans want change in Washington, and Democrats need new leadership to deliver that

There have been murmurings of a possible leadership challenge in re...
body_text:
Senator Van Hollen says midterm results show Americans want change in Washington, and Democrats need new leadership to deliver that

There have been murmurings of a possible leadership challenge in recent days, with a number of Democrats questioning whether Schumer is the right person to lead the party into its next chapter.

Among the most outspoken was Kansas senator-elect Adam Hamilton, who warned Schumer was seen by many people in his state as a “polarising” and “divisive” figure.

“What I’d be looking for is a leader who can lead from the centre,” he told NBC on Sunday. “Somebody who can bring Republicans and Democrats together, somebody who can bring the various factions in the Democratic party together. Somebody with fresh ideas.

“No disrespect for Chuck Schumer, just it feels like it is a time for fresh and new ideas and somebody who can unite us instead of dividing us.”

Senator Elissa Slotkin, of Michigan, has also made clear she does not support Schumer as leader.

“I think whoever wants to run this caucus should come forward with a plan on how they’re going to govern differently, what they’re going to do in the first 100 days to put money in people’s pockets and then in particular how they’re going to communicate differently,” Slotkin said on Tuesday, adding that she was not actively seeking the position herself.

Speaking alongside her at the joint press conference, independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, praised Schumer’s role in the party’s success in the midterms but argued such victories should not entitle him to another term in the leadership.

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer,” Sanders said.

“But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be re-elected as the Democratic leader.”

Good morning, and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Barely a week after sweeping to a stunning midterm victory, Democrats have found themselves facing an altogether different battle, one within their own ranks.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has launched a challenge to Chuck Schumer, of New York, for the Senate’s top Democratic leadership post. Announcing his decision during an interview with MS Now last night, Van Hollen argued that last week’s midterm election results showed Americans wanted a fundamental change in Washington, and that Democrats needed new leadership in order to deliver that.

double quotation markWe saw a huge outburst of democracy on election day – red states, blue states, purple states – and it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption, his wars and his cruelty, it was also about a call for a larger change, to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favour of the very wealthy against working people, and it’s fuelled by a corrupt political system.

The call was to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual, and to do that, I think we need new leadership.”

His challenge came just days after Democrats secured control of the Senate, winning at least 55 seats in what has been a remarkable election cycle for the party. Winning the leadership contest requires a majority of the caucus, about 28 or 29 senators, with an election scheduled for next month.

The caucus votes behind closed doors by secret ballot, but Van Hollen told MS Now that he had the support of “more than 10” Democratic senators.

Progressive heavyweight Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont who caucuses with the Democrats, has already publicly declared he will not support Schumer, saying “the time is now for change”. Endorsing Van Hollen, Sanders said: “The American people voted for change. They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families.”

Incoming Democratic senator Abdul El-Sayed, of Michigan, has also openly backed Van Hollen, saying he was “proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority”.

double quotation markThe American public spoke clearly last week. They rejected Trumpism. But we have yet to earn our mandate. That will require bold leadership. I called [Van Hollen] to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience. We need both right now.”

Responding to Van Hollen’s leadership bid, Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since January 2017, said he welcomed “a discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead”, but that he had the votes to be re-elected as leader.

title: Sen Bernie Sanders supports Chris Van Hollen's bid to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader post
excerpt:
Fox News host Sean Hannity reports on Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., announcing his challenge to Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for Senate majority leader on ‘Hannity.’

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., is bac...
body_text:
Fox News host Sean Hannity reports on Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., announcing his challenge to Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for Senate majority leader on ‘Hannity.’

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., is backing Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., for the role of Senate Democratic leader.

"The American people voted for change. They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families. That is why I am supporting Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats," Sanders said in a Thursday post on X.

Van Hollen threw his hat into the ring for the role on Thursday, mounting a challenge against current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who is looking to retain the Senate Democratic leader position to serve as Senate majority leader next year.

"In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption. To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn't about any one person – it’s about answering that call. That's why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader," Van Hollen said in a Thursday post on X.

VAN HOLLEN CHALLENGES SCHUMER FOR SENATE LEADERSHIP AFTER DEMOCRATIC ELECTION SWEEP

U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol Building on Nov. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Schumer asserted in a post that he has the support to retain his leadership position: "I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people."

Sanders had said during a Tuesday press conference that he would not support Schumer for re-election as Senate Democratic leader.

During an interview on an episode of "The Weekly Show with Jon Stewart," Sanders said that he would support Van Hollen if he decided to run for the role.

DEMOCRATS TURN ON SCHUMER AFTER HISTORIC ELECTION WINS AS POTENTIAL CHALLENGER EMERGES

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks during a Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies hearing in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, May 12, 2026. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated President Donald Trump-backed former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan's 2026 U.S. Senate contest, is also backing Van Hollen.

"The American public spoke clearly last week. They rejected Trumpism. But we have yet to earn our mandate. That will require bold leadership. I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience. We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority," El-Sayed wrote in a Thursday post on X when sharing Van Hollen's announcement.

BERNIE SANDERS SAYS HE WON'T BACK SCHUMER AS PUSH FOR NEW LEADERSHIP GAINS STEAM

Republican National Committee national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement posted on X that "Chris Van Hollen cares more about a Salvadoran gang member than working families. This leadership brawl previews the D.C. Democrats' agenda: chaos, infighting, and a race to see who can sell their soul to the far left fastest. Whoever is the winner gets to lead the charge to open our borders, shred our Constitution, and treat taxpayers like bottomless ATMs."

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: JonBenet Ramsey investigators are retesting evidence with newer technology, police chief says
excerpt: Boulder Police Chief Steve Redfearn and District Attorney Michael Dougherty say old evidence is being retested with state-of-the-art technology as JonBenet Ramsey's unsolved murder nears the 30-year m...
body_text:
Boulder Police Chief Steve Redfearn and District Attorney Michael Dougherty say old evidence is being retested with state-of-the-art technology as JonBenet Ramsey's unsolved murder nears the 30-year mark.

Investigators in Boulder are retesting decades-old evidence in the murder of JonBenet Ramsey as her family nears 30 years since the unsolved slaying in their former Colorado home.

"Chief [Steve] Redfearn and I are more hopeful now than we have been in the past because of the advances in the investigation and the advances in technology," Boulder County District Attorney Michael Dougherty told reporters in a news briefing this week. "And I say that based on just how DNA has progressed over time."

Her father, John Ramsey, had spent years begging authorities to attempt to solve the case through investigative genetic genealogy, a relatively new technique for ginning up DNA leads that involves combining genetic testing results with genealogy research to identify potential persons of interest. IGG itself is rapidly evolving as state-of-the-art DNA testing also improves.

JONBENET RAMSEY'S FATHER ASKS TRUMP FOR HELP IN DAUGHTER'S UNSOLVED MURDER CASE

JonBenet Patricia Ramsey, 4, lies on a white seamless backdrop wearing white lace gloves during a studio session for a commercial ad and actress portfolio in Boulder, Colo., on May 1, 1994. (ZUMAPRESS.com)

A cold case review panel was convened in Boulder as local police, state and federal investigators continue to dig into what happened on Dec. 26, 1996, when JonBenet was found strangled and with head trauma in the basement of her home. Although investigators have pursued a number of potential suspects, persons of interest and theories about how she died over the years, no one has been convicted, and her death remains one of America's most prominent unsolved cases.

"It's no secret," Boulder Police Chief Steve Redfearn told reporters in a sit-down interview earlier this week. "We're also going back, based on that cold case review, and retesting things that were tested 30 years ago with newer technology."

MICHAEL RUIZ: JONBENÉT RAMSEY'S FATHER CHALLENGES DA AFTER REPORT SAYS FAMILY SHOULDN'T HAVE BEEN CLEARED

Boulder Police Chief Steve Redfearn and District Attorney Michael Dougherty speak with reporters at a news briefing on the JonBenet Ramsey case in November 2026. The Colorado 6-year-old's 1996 murder remains unsolved. (City of Boulder)

Redfearn appeared to confirm a recent revelation from JonBenet's half-brother, John Andrew Ramsey, who told Fox News Digital previously that the family had learned this year that new testing had begun in the fall of 2025.

"Maybe something comes of that," Redfearn said. "Not that it was missed, but maybe the technology just improved enough that we look at, hey, this item was tested in '97, we're testing it again, and hey, look, we found something that was missed in '97."

Dougherty gave an example of a recent trial that he said involved the testimony of four different DNA experts because testing had been done on multiple occasions as the technology improved.

Among the benefits of rapidly improving technology is an increasingly successful ability to identify DNA profiles contained in mixed samples, Dougherty added.

"To me, it's quantity, quality, and location of the DNA," he said.

Traditionally, testing a sample left behind by a single donor is straightforward, he explained.

"When it's a single source in DNA, just generally speaking, it's much easier assuming you have enough to test, particularly if it's blood or semen," he said. "But if it's touch, and it's a single source, that's different than if it's touch or saliva, and it is a mixture."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

JonBenet Ramsey pictured in an undated portrait. The 6-year-old was found dead in her home on Dec. 26, 1996, in one of America's most high-profile unsolved cases. (Splash News)

When two or more people leave DNA on the same surface, it must first be untangled in a lab.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

The process can be destructive to the evidence, especially when there isn't much left, he said, and that complicates things under evidence rules that must be validated and stand up in court.

"We're not gonna do it recklessly, to use Chief Redfearn's word," Dougherty said. "We're also not gonna hesitate. We recognize the clock's ticking. None of us are gonna be here forever. We wanna see this case solved for everyone involved and everyone impacted by it. And we're absolutely committed to doing that."

John Ramsey speaks with Fox News Digital in Las Vegas in April 2022. He is the father of JonBenet Ramsey, the 6-year-old whose murder on Dec. 26, 1996, remains unsolved nearly 30 years later. (Michael Ruiz/Fox News Digital)

JONBENET RAMSEY CASE: FATHER REMEMBERS 'DADDY'S GIRL' ON WHAT WOULD BE HER 32ND BIRTHDAY

Separately, Redfearn told reporters that if the new DNA testing fails to yield results, investigators have additional previously unreleased evidence they could make public in the hope that someone comes forward.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"There’s still plenty of things that are not out there that we have," he told reporters.

While tips continue to come in regularly almost three decades after JonBenet's slaying, investigators are still asking anyone who may have information to come forward.

"There is more than one someone out there that knows something," Redfearn said.
